rationale: The entry’s central claim is not merely that Sabbath connotes rest, but that in counting contexts it can name a complete seven structured by a concluding rest. The strongest alternative treats the week-sense as a secondary metonymy from the seventh-day Sabbath. That alternative is linguistically plausible, but it does not explain the combined evidence better: Leviticus 23:15 and Deuteronomy 16:9 use “seven sabbaths” and “seven weeks” for the same statutory count; Leviticus 25 scales the expression to seven-year units and seven such units; and the Greek idioms in Luke 18:12 and Matthew 28:1 indisputably use sabbaton language for a week. The book’s identification accommodates both the rest-day sense and these unit-counting senses by treating rest as the completing member. No supplied detail contradicts that account or is explainable only by the counter-reading. The entry does not assert the chapter’s more speculative calendar or millennial applications, so those do not reduce its support scope.
book_core_identification: Sabbath names a complete, rest-crowned unit of seven—not merely an isolated rest day—with the rest functioning as the completing member of the whole.
book_secondary_elaborations: The Sabbath unit appears at multiple legal scales: the ordinary week, the land’s seventh-year cycle, and the seven sevens counted toward Jubilee.
Leviticus’ “seven sabbaths” and Deuteronomy’s “seven weeks” designate the same span.
Greek sabbaton can designate a week, as in “twice in the sabbath” meaning twice a week.
The resurrection expression mia sabbatōn designates the first day of the week as “one of the sabbaths.”
chapter_only_objections: The chapter’s claim that yom ha-shabbat proves that shabbat fundamentally names a unit rather than a day is not decisive; genitival day-expressions need not encode that semantic distinction.

The argument that shabbat shabbaton specifically marks the resting member, while undoubled shabbat marks the whole unit, requires broader lexical validation and is not established merely by the cited contrasts.
The claim that the six workdays are themselves commanded as constituent parts of the Sabbath goes beyond what the six-and-one formulas necessarily establish.
The proposed lunar calendar of four sevens with renewed-moon days outside the weeks is highly contestable and is not established by the glossary entry’s references.
The six-thousand-year labor followed by a thousand-year Sabbath depends on a disputed chronological use of 2 Peter 3:8 and is not asserted in the glossary entry.
strongest_counter_interpretation: Shabbat primarily denotes cessation or the marked rest day (and, by extension, a sabbatical rest year); its use for a week is a conventional metonymy in which the whole period is named after its distinctive Sabbath day. Thus the cited Hebrew and Greek counting idioms establish an extended week-sense but not that the complete seven is the word’s fundamental symbolic referent.
counter_core_identification: The Sabbath’s primary referent is the marked period of cessation or rest, especially the seventh day; references to a week or seven-year cycle are secondary extensions from that marked resting member.
material_core_denial: The counter denies that the complete seven is the Sabbath’s governing identification, treating the attested week-sense as metonymic rather than as evidence that rest is the completing member of the unit named Sabbath.
counter_case: The noun is associated with the verb shavat, “cease,” naturally favoring cessation or rest as its primary semantic center.
Many conduct passages apply Sabbath directly to the seventh day on which work ceases.
Luke 18:12 and mia sabbatōn can be explained as established idioms in which the marked Sabbath day lends its name to the week.
Leviticus 25 can be read as calling each seventh, resting year a Sabbath and then counting seven such sabbatical years, without making Sabbath the name of each full seven-year block.
book_explanatory_advantages: It directly unifies the parallel statutory expressions “seven sabbaths” and “seven weeks” rather than treating their equivalence as an unexplained lexical accident.
It explains why sabbath terminology functions naturally in both day-based and year-based counts.
It gives a single account of the Greek week idioms and the seventh-day sense: the word can name the whole unit and its crowning member.
It incorporates Hebrews 4:9’s continuing Sabbath-rest without reducing the term to bare inactivity.
counter_explanatory_advantages: It accords readily with the etymological association with cessation and with ordinary passages regulating behavior on the seventh day.
Metonymy from a marked day to its surrounding week is a familiar linguistic mechanism and therefore requires no specialized semantic system.
It better reflects the possibility that different contexts employ related but distinct lexical senses rather than one uniform symbolic definition.
decisive_sources: Leviticus 23:15 with Deuteronomy 16:9: the same festival count is expressed as seven sabbaths and seven weeks.
Leviticus 25:2-8: Sabbath terminology operates at the year scale and in the forty-nine-year count.
Luke 18:12: dis tou sabbatou means twice per week.
Matthew 28:1: sabbaton language occurs with both the Sabbath day and the first day of the week.
Hebrews 4:9: Sabbath-rest remains the completing rest toward which the preceding labor moves.
unresolved_objections: The evidence establishes a genuine week-sense more securely than it establishes that this is the word’s fundamental meaning in every context.
The metonymic account remains viable and may be preferred in conventional lexicography, even though it does not outperform the book on the supplied cross-text pattern.
The phrase “at every scale the law counts” is supported by the day- and year-scale examples supplied but should not be generalized beyond those demonstrated scales without further evidence.
